summary: Experience showed that 6to4, an IPv6 transition mechanism from RFC 3056, works poorly when used in its anycast mode across the open Internet. This document deprecates the anycast prefix for 6to4 relay routers defined in RFC 3068 and recommends against using anycast 6to4. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A shortcut that helped people move from the old road system to the new one turned out to cause traffic jams and wrong turns. This note says to stop using that shortcut.

subtitle: Why the anycast form of 6to4 was deprecated, and what operators and implementers should do instead.

tldr.problem: The anycast form of 6to4, defined in RFC 3068, proved to have severe practical problems on the Internet. High failure rates led some end users to disable IPv6, and some content providers to hold back from offering IPv6 content.
tldr.mechanism: The document deprecates anycast 6to4 and the address 192.88.99.1, deprecates 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels, and requires 6to4 to be disabled by default. Unicast 6to4 and the prefix 2002::/16 are not deprecated.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3068 and RFC 6732, asks that they move to Historic status, and reserves 192.88.99.0/24 against reuse except by an IETF Standards Action.

today: RFC 7526 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 196) published in May 2015, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It obsoletes RFC 3068 and RFC 6732, so the anycast form of 6to4 should not be used or newly built into products.

sections.title: Why Anycast 6to4 Is Deprecated
sections.content:
The original 6to4 transition mechanism (RFC 3056) uses unicast addressing. Its extension, RFC 3068, adds an anycast prefix for 6to4 relay routers, and that extension has shown severe practical problems on the Internet. This document asks that RFC 3068 and RFC 6732 be moved to Historic status.

6to4 was meant to help the move from IPv4 to IPv6 and has been a good way to experiment with IPv6. But because of the high failure rates seen with anycast 6to4, end users may disable IPv6 on their hosts, which has made some content providers reluctant to offer IPv6 content.

Advice in RFC 6343 to disable 6to4 by default has been widely adopted in recent operating systems, and many browsers hide the failures by using Happy Eyeballs (RFC 6555). Even so, IPv6 content providers still see a measurable amount of 6to4 traffic, and operational failures have continued. The remaining successful users are likely on hosts that use the obsolete policy table of RFC 3484 (which prefers 6to4 over IPv4) and lack Happy Eyeballs.
sections.plainLanguage: The shortcut often failed, so people gave up on the new roads altogether. Computers have already learned to switch it off, but some old ones still try it.

sections.title: 6to4 and Its Operational Problems
sections.content:
6to4 lets isolated IPv6 islands reach each other using automatic IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling. To reach the native IPv6 Internet it relies on relay routers in both directions. In the forward direction, a 6to4 node sends IPv4-encapsulated IPv6 traffic to a relay connected to both the 6to4 cloud and native IPv6. In the reverse direction, a 2002::/16 route is injected into the native IPv6 routing domain to attract traffic to a relay. Different relays are expected in each direction.

One deployment model in Section 5.2 of RFC 3056 has a 6to4 router keep managed (BGP) connections to a set of relays. That controls the forward path but does not guarantee a working reverse path, and it carries the same operational burden as manually configured tunnels, with no deployment seen in the public Internet.

RFC 3068 adds a well-known IPv4 anycast address to reach the nearest relay in the forward direction. Its operational problems are described in Section 3 of RFC 6343. The document also notes that peer-to-peer use of 6to4 exists, is harmless to third parties and does not depend on anycast 6to4.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic needs a helper to cross between the old and new networks. The anycast trick sent you to whichever helper was nearest, but that helper might not actually be working.

sections.title: What Is and Is Not Deprecated
sections.content:
The document formally deprecates the anycast 6to4 mechanism of RFC 3068 and its anycast IPv4 address 192.88.99.1, which is no longer considered a useful service of last resort. The prefix 192.88.99.0/24 MUST NOT be reassigned for other use except by a future IETF Standards Action.

The basic unicast 6to4 mechanism of RFC 3056 and the prefix 2002::/16 are not deprecated, and the default address selection rules of RFC 6724 are not modified. Because anycast 6to4 is gone, 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels (RFC 6732) are no longer needed and are also deprecated.

Here, "deprecate" is used only in its generic sense of criticize or express disapproval, with no specific normative meaning, and a deprecated function may stay in the Internet for years for backwards compatibility. Other IETF documents that mention 6to4 incidentally should be reviewed, and the references possibly removed, when they are next updated.
sections.plainLanguage: The risky shortcut is retired and its special address is locked up. The ordinary version of the trick is still allowed.

sections.title: Implementation Recommendations
sections.content:
It is NOT RECOMMENDED to include anycast 6to4 in new implementations. If it is included, it MUST be disabled by default.

In host implementations, unicast 6to4 MUST also be disabled by default, and hosts using 6to4 MUST support the address-selection policy of RFC 6724. In router implementations, 6to4 MUST be disabled by default, and enabling IPv6 forwarding on a device MUST NOT automatically enable 6to4.
sections.plainLanguage: New devices should ship with the shortcut switched off, and turning on IPv6 should never switch it on by accident.

sections.title: Operational Recommendations
sections.content:
The document does not recommend generalized filtering of 6to4 or anycast 6to4 traffic or routes. It recommends against further deployment of anycast 6to4 and asks current operators to evaluate whether continued use is worthwhile.

Networks SHOULD NOT filter packets with source address 192.88.99.1, since that is normal traffic from a 6to4 return relay. This includes letting a local return relay's traffic through anti-spoofing filters (RFC 2827, RFC 3704) and uRPF checks (RFC 5635).

Operators of an anycast relay at 192.88.99.1 SHOULD review RFC 6343 and this document, and consider whether the relay can be discontinued as traffic diminishes. Providers that only route to 192.88.99.1 SHOULD verify that it leads to a working relay, and providers MUST NOT originate a route to it unless they actively operate and monitor an anycast 6to4 relay. Operators of return relays answering for 2002::/16 SHOULD similarly consider discontinuing them, and providers SHOULD announce 2002::/16 to their customers if and only if it leads to a correctly operating return relay. IPv6-only providers, including those running NAT64, are advised that their customers need a route to such a relay in case a residual 6to4 user elsewhere tries to reach them. Operators of 6to4 Provider Managed Tunnels SHOULD consider when to discontinue them.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not block the replies coming back from old helpers, and only keep a helper running if it really works. If it is not needed any more, shut it down.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IANA IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry (RFC 6890) listed the 6to4 Relay Anycast prefix 192.88.99.0/24. IANA has marked it "Deprecated (6to4 Relay Anycast)", added a reference to this RFC and removed the Boolean values for the block. Redelegating the prefix for any use requires justification via an IETF Standards Action.

The document says there are no new security considerations. General security issues with tunnels are listed in RFC 6169, and issues specific to 6to4 in RFC 3964 and RFC 6324.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of special addresses now says this one is retired and cannot be handed out again without a proper decision.
